title: Different roads
hook: by different means we reach the same end: sometimes mercy softens an enemy, sometimes courage (Essays 1.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the runaway horse: Montaigne's idle mind bolting, and his pen following it. Your line was the runaway horse.

Same fight, same parent, two different kids. One cries and says sorry, and the parent melts. The other stands there, chin up, and says, I did it, and I'd do it again, and somehow the parent melts for that one too. Montaigne opens the whole book of Essays with this, in the very first chapter, though his examples are a good deal bloodier: a conqueror at the gates of a town, and the question of what makes him stop.
screen: `ONE SAYS SORRY.` → `ONE STANDS FIRM.` → `BOTH ARE FORGIVEN.`

segments.voice: First, the usual road. The title says it: by different means we arrive at the same end. When someone we've wronged has us in their power, Montaigne says, the common way to soften them is to give in and move them to pity. Second, the other road. Sometimes the opposite works: courage and steadiness. His first story is a prince at the sack of a town. The people, the women and the children, throw themselves at his feet, and he isn't moved. Then he sees three gentlemen holding their ground against his whole army with astonishing boldness, and that is what stops his anger. He spares them, and then the town. Third, the surprise in the middle. Montaigne turns it on himself. He'd be the one swayed by pity, he says, and more easily by pity than by admiration, though he knows the Stoics counted pity a fault. So the essay isn't a rule. It's two roads and two different hearts. Fourth, the line that sends the whole book on its way. Man, he writes, is a marvelously vain, varied, and wavering thing; it's hard to build any steady judgment on him. The essays after it keep trying to catch that wavering thing. And it fits the week: a village content at home, true words without polish, the Tao's close, a tower, painted beams, a runaway horse. Different roads into the same quiet work. Close to home, an approach that failed with one person might be the wrong road, not the wrong goal.
screen: `THE USUAL ROAD: PITY.` · `THE OTHER ROAD: COURAGE.` · `MONTAIGNE, MOVED BY PITY.` · `A WAVERING THING.` · then, large: `DIFFERENT ROADS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where you keep taking the same road and getting the same result: a conversation with a teenager, a habit you keep trying to quit, a coworker who won't budge. Is your usual road soft or firm, talking or waiting? Picture the other road, just once, and see where it might go.
Different roads. Montaigne's first essay: by different means we reach the same end; sometimes pity softens a conqueror, sometimes courage does. Today's word.
Your line: different roads. The goal can stay put while the way changes. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some readers of Montaigne take the first chapter of the Essays as a key to the whole book: people are too varied for one rule, so the same end can be reached by opposite means.

fork.setup: you're the prince at the sack of the town. the people beg at your feet. then you see three men standing firm against your army. what moves you?
fork.reveal: in Montaigne's story the pleas didn't move him, but the boldness of the three gentlemen stopped his anger, and he spared them and then the town.

original.note: French: by different means we arrive at the same end, the title of Montaigne's first essay.

trapdoor: what you thought: different roads means there's more than one way to do things.
what it means: people are moved by opposite things, pity or courage, so no single approach always works.
what a scholar hears: the first essay ends on man as a vain, varied, wavering subject, a line some readers take as the theme of the whole book.
guess: different means, like pity or courage, can reach one end
choosing one firm rule and keeping it in every situation
leaving home to travel and see how other people live

chat.says: When someone's angry with you, should you say sorry or stand firm?
options: Montaigne says it depends: pity softens some people, courage softens others.
Montaigne says always stand firm, since saying sorry only shows weakness.
Montaigne says always apologize, since courage only makes people angrier.
chat.meaning: His first essay: by different means we arrive at the same end. A prince unmoved by pleas spared a town for three gentlemen's boldness.
